title: Record prices. Cash flow still has to deliver.
deck: My read after Tuesday’s close: lower yields helped the valuation backdrop, but the rally was not universal and services costs remain a constraint. Google’s nuclear-power agreement shows how demand can become contracted revenue; the investment question is how much cash remains after building the capacity.

sections.title: A record is not the same as broad participation.
sections.body: AP reported gains of 0.5% for the Dow and 0.4% for the Nasdaq Composite, while the Russell 2000 fell 0.6%. Treasury’s two-year par yield fell five basis points to 4.79%; ten years fell four to 5.27%, and thirty years two to 5.64%. My interpretation: lower nominal yields offered valuation relief, but small-cap weakness cautions against calling this an economy-wide improvement. That comparison is a breadth clue, not a full advance/decline analysis. A single session cannot establish either a lasting change in financing conditions or the cause of the stock-market gains.

sections.title: Demand is growing; so is pressure on margins.
sections.body: ISM’s September services report, released on 5 October, put its headline PMI at 54.9 versus 55.4 in August. New orders remained expansionary at 59.8, while the prices index rose to 74.0 from 72.6. My assessment: this combination is more consistent with continued demand and difficult cost control than with a clean disinflation story. These are diffusion indexes, not percentage growth in output or prices. The counterargument is that sustained orders and pricing power may protect profits. That needs confirmation in realized margins and cash conversion; higher selling prices alone would not demonstrate stronger real demand.

sections.title: An electricity contract is not free cash flow.
sections.body: Constellation announced a 20-year agreement with Google supporting 890 MW of additional nuclear capacity and more than $4.3 billion of investment; the first uprate is expected by 2028. A separate 15-year agreement covers 2,700 MW from existing generation. Those are different commitments: not all contracted power is new capacity. My inference: a long-duration buyer can improve revenue visibility and support investment. But the announcement does not disclose enough pricing and cost detail to establish project returns. Construction overruns, outages and financing costs could absorb the benefit. The bullish case is successful delivery with attractive contracted margins; it should be tested rather than inferred from megawatts alone.

sections.title: Test cash generation before rewarding the story.
sections.body: For a normalized operating business, use the DCF to compare weaker free-cash-flow growth with a higher WACC, separately and together. Do not mechanically translate one day’s Treasury move into an equal change in WACC. In the LBO Deal Lab, reduce the EBITDA margin or increase capex while holding the exit multiple fixed; this isolates the effect on debt repayment. Neither calculator is a construction-stage nuclear-project model: phased spending, delayed commissioning and contract-specific pricing need a separate forecast. Better realized margins and sustained financing relief would strengthen the optimistic case; delayed cash receipts or cost overruns would weaken it.

watch: Watch whether smaller-company performance begins to confirm the large-index rally across several sessions, rather than treating one record close as broad strength.
Compare upcoming company results with the services survey: can revenue growth translate into stable margins and operating cash flow?
Look for disclosed power-contract economics, spending schedules and delivery milestones before converting announced capacity into a return estimate.
caveat: Codex’s analysis, not Owen’s personal view or investment advice. Research completed at the actual ET/HKT cutoff above, later than the scheduled run. Market closes and the cited Treasury web-table observations cover 6 October, the latest completed US cash session. This is not a live feed. Treasury daily par yields are indicative, not executable quotes; equity percentage moves are rounded. ISM describes September conditions and was released on 5 October, not during Tuesday’s session. Company capacity, investment and delivery figures are announced plans, not completed assets or guaranteed returns. Interpretations are conditional and do not prove causality. Calculator examples are educational, not valuations of Constellation or financing offers.
